_what_this_is: The signed file that tells every customer's copy of Maven BabelFish which version of each reading application has been published. It is fetched from this exact address, over https, by the machine that holds a customer's account, and checked against a Ghost Labs public half compiled into the product. See docs/RELEASES_FORMAT.md in the BabelFish repository for the field table.
_what_this_file_is_not: This is a placeholder and it is not a signed releases file. It names no platform and carries no signature, because nothing has been published to a customer yet and because the key that signs one lives on the encrypted drive and never in a repository. It is here so that the address is live, correct and served over https while nothing depends on it, which is exactly why the empty appcast beside it is published before the first release rather than after.
_what_a_machine_does_with_it_today: Nothing fetches it. No build that has shipped carries a Ghost Labs releases key, and a build that cannot check what comes back makes no request at all. A machine that somehow did fetch this would refuse it for having no signature, write one line in its log, and go on announcing whatever its own build was born knowing. Nothing stops either way: a releases file announces a version and stops nothing.
_what_must_happen_before_anything_fetche: Replace this with a real one, minted and signed, BEFORE releases_public is ever pinned into a shipped build - because pinning that key is the moment every install in the world starts fetching this address. Mint it on the machine where the signing key is: tools/support/ghost_labs_support.py releases --key <the mounted drive>/releases.key --macos <version> --macos-where <a page a person can open>. Then copy the file it writes over this one, at this same path, and push.
_why_replacing_it_is_safe_and_late_is_no: Publishing it late costs nothing and publishing nothing costs nothing: every customer's machine goes on announcing whatever it last knew about, and a reader that is told nothing says nothing rather than being told it is up to date. What is not safe is moving it. This address is compiled into every copy that has ever shipped.
